findings.title: A chain that was sealed but never OPENED terminates the crossing and silently discards all offset history before it
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED end-to-end through LocalSequencer on the isolated staged tree. pod1 starts at epoch 1 and acks 7 records at 0..6. pod2 acquires epoch 2, seals chain 1, then fails writing chain 2's CONTINUE -- the exact path LocalSequencerFailoverTest.aStartThatFailsAFTERAcquiringHandsTheLeaseBackRatherThanStrandingIt already exercises with RefuseKeyStore -- so start's catch releases the lease and chain 2 is left EMPTY. pod3 acquires epoch 3. recoverChainEnd on the empty chain 2 returns lastKey==null -> nextSequence 0, so seal() writes Seal(0, continuedAt=3) at slot 0 and prevSeq=0. pod3 opens chain 3 with CONTINUE(0, 2, 0) and crossFrom(2,0) walks chain 2, reads the Seal at slot 0, finds no CONTINUE to follow, and returns with an empty offset map. Chain 1's 7 records are unreachable forever. Probe output: 'PROBE pod2 failed as designed: injected: the store refused .../0000000000000002/0000000000000000.delta', 'PROBE pod3 epoch = 3', 'PROBE pod3 firstOffset = 0' -- expected 7. Offsets are reassigned across a failover: I2, NFR-11, and M4 acceptance criterion 4, which is the exact defect this task exists to close. Any IOException between leases.tryAcquire() and log.open() (a transient store error on recoverChainEnd, seal, recover or open) manufactures this state, and start's release-on-failure branch is a designed path, not a rare crash window. Confirmed independently at the CommitLog layer: chain 1 = [CONTINUE, delta(100 records), SEAL@2], chain 2 = [SEAL@0], chain 3 = [CONTINUE(0,2,0)] -> reader at epoch 3 reports nextOffset 0 where 100 is correct. Neither CommitLogCrossEpochTest nor LocalSequencerFailoverTest builds a chain sealed at slot 0, so nothing in the suite sees it.

findings.title: MAX_CHAIN_DEPTH bounds legitimate leadership HISTORY, not corruption; at 1002 terms the sequencer becomes permanently unelectable and the error blames the bytes
findings.failure_scenario: The stated justification is false. 'A CONTINUE may only ever name a LOWER epoch, so a chain deeper than 1000 is corrupt bytes rather than long history' -- monotonically decreasing epochs bound the depth by the EPOCH NUMBER, not by 1000. Lease.takenOverBy does epoch+1 on every acquisition and LeaseManager never resets or compacts it, and LocalSequencer.start writes a CONTINUE naming E-1 on every term, so after N takeovers the legitimate chain is N-1 deep. MEASURED on the staged tree with a well-formed history of [CONTINUE, delta, SEAL] per term: terms=1001 recovers correctly (nextOffset=1001); terms=1002 throws 'CONTINUE chain deeper than 1000 at epoch 1; a chain may only name a LOWER epoch, so this is corrupt rather than long'. Every takeover burns an epoch -- pod restart, rolling deploy, TTL expiry, and every failed start (which releases and lets the next acquirer mint E+1) -- so 1002 arrives with certainty, not as an anomaly. When it does, log.open throws inside start, start releases the lease and rethrows, the next node acquires E+1 and hits the same wall: the cluster can never elect a sequencer again, with no recovery path, and the operator is told the object store holds corrupt bytes when it holds a correct history. The same false justification is committed to the M4.6e backlog row ('TRANSITIVE across several terms, and bounded -- a CONTINUE may only ever name a LOWER epoch, so a chain deeper than 1000 is corrupt bytes rather than long history').

findings.title: Takeover request count grows with the NUMBER OF PRIOR TERMS, and the relaxed cost test pins only the predecessor-length dimension
findings.failure_scenario: The crossing is transitive to epoch 1, so every takeover re-reads the FULL contents of every ancestor chain, not just the predecessor's. MEASURED on the staged tree with a constant 12 deltas per term, counting the last takeover through CountingBinStore: 1 prior term -> 16 GETs / 3 LISTs; 2 -> 30/4; 4 -> 58/6; 8 -> 114/10; 16 -> 226/18. That is a per-failover request count of O(all commit-log entries ever written) = O(total segments committed over the cluster's lifetime), growing without bound, on the path whose entire purpose is restoring sequencing quickly -- and one LIST per ancestor chain, so the LIST count grows with terms too. The test relaxes isEqualTo(2L) to linear and claims 'WHAT MUST NOT REGRESS FURTHER is the SLOPE' and 'anything super-linear ... fails here', but BOTH its data points (12 entries -> 16, 40 entries -> 44) hold the epoch count at exactly 2, so the dominant growth dimension is unconstrained: a change that made the crossing read every ancestor twice, or that added a per-ancestor probe, passes both assertions unchanged. A third fixture varying the number of TERMS at a fixed chain length is what would pin what actually matters. Per non-negotiable 2 and cost.md, a cost threshold moved in the weakening direction must be replaced by one that constrains the real dimension, and this one does not.

findings.title: The class javadoc still asserts the gap this commit closes, and was not updated
findings.failure_scenario: The staged LocalSequencer class javadoc reads 'OFFSETS RESTART AT 0 ON EVERY TAKEOVER, and this class does not yet honour the contract it implements ... M4.6e closes it by following the CONTINUE across the boundary; until then a multi-term deployment violates I2'. M4.6e is THIS commit, and the same commit adds LocalSequencerFailoverTest.OFFSETSSURVIVEAFailoverEndToEnd asserting firstOffset 10 after a failover -- so the production entry point's own javadoc now contradicts the test beside it. The concrete cost: M4.6d is BLOCKED ON M4.6e precisely because of this gap; its author reads this javadoc, believes offset continuity is still absent, and either re-implements the crossing or leaves the block in place. The M4.6c backlog row states the governing rule for the mirror-image case -- 'A row naming work it does not deliver is the same defect as a comment claiming a mechanism it does not have' -- and a comment denying a mechanism the class now has is the same defect with the sign flipped.

findings.title: The justification for relaxing the cost threshold cites an M4.9 backlog change that this diff does not make
findings.failure_scenario: The comment carrying the weakened cost assertion states 'M4.8's checkpoints and M4.9's bounded recovery are what make this constant again, and M4.9's row now says it must bound the CROSSING and not merely own-chain replay.' The staged backlog diff touches only the M4.6e row and adds M0.67; M4.9's row is unchanged and reads in full 'Bounded recovery: newest checkpoint + at most K deltas, replacing today's unbounded full-chain replay. Asserted by REQUEST COUNT through CountingBinStore ... Also tier 3 of M5's fallback ladder' -- it says nothing about the crossing. So the future work that is offered as the reason a forbidden threshold relaxation is acceptable does not exist anywhere in the tree, and the M4.9 author will scope bounded recovery to own-chain replay and leave P3's unbounded ancestor walk in place. This is a mechanism asserted rather than executed, in the one comment whose whole job is to carry a non-negotiable-2 exception.

findings.title: The delta-to-offset folding rule now exists in two places
findings.failure_scenario: ChainReplay.applyOffsets and CommitLog.apply both compute 'merge(run.key(), run.lastOffset() + 1, Math::max)'. The split's own stated principle -- 'ADDRESSING COMES FROM CommitLog, never re-derived here ... a second copy would be a wire-format duplication waiting to drift' -- was applied to the key grammar but not to the offset rule, which is equally wire-semantics. If a future change makes lastOffset exclusive, or adds a run field affecting the next offset, updating only CommitLog.apply leaves the crossing reader computing a different history from the writer, and the disagreement surfaces only after a failover.
